reading.rtitle: Why Executives Choose the Passive Voice
paras: In an executive memo, the shape of a sentence decides what the reader notices first. In the active voice, the person comes first: 'My team streamlined the approval process.' In the passive voice, the result comes first: 'The approval process was streamlined.' Both sentences are true; they simply point the light at different places. Executives choose the passive when the decision, the impact, or the deliverable matters more than the name of the person who did the work.

The passive is built the same way in every tense: a form of 'be' plus the past participle. 'The rationale is explained in the first paragraph.' 'The issue was escalated to the vice president.' 'Two deliverables have been completed.' 'Every new model must be reviewed before release.' If you want to name the person, you add 'by': 'The framework was designed by the safety team.' If the doer is obvious, unknown, or simply not the point, you leave it out -- and that is when the passive is most useful.

There is a limit. The passive can hide who is responsible, and a good reader notices. 'Mistakes were made' is famous exactly because nobody is named. Strong leaders use the passive for precision, not for cover. They use it to keep results, oversight, and credit in focus, and they switch back to the active voice the moment a decision has to be attributed to a real person -- including themselves.

gapfill.text: The passive is always be + past participle: is explained, was streamlined, have been completed, must be reviewed. The tense changes on 'be' only -- the participle never changes. Add 'by + person' when the doer is the point: 'The framework was designed by four engineers.'

bank.label: Useful sentences for a quarterly update

forms.title: The passive across tenses: be + past participle
cards: Present -- a routine or a rule
'The rationale is explained in the first paragraph.' Use it for what happens every time.
'The issue was escalated to the vice president.' Use it for what was done and when.
'Two deliverables have been completed.' Use it when a past result still matters today.
'Every new model must be reviewed before release.' The modal carries the force; 'be' never changes.
'The decision will be escalated to the board next week.'

items.situation: Your team made the approval process simpler last quarter. Report the result without naming anyone.
tips: The approval process was streamlined last quarter.
Two weeks were cut from the cycle.

items.situation: A board member asks who is responsible for a delay. Give the cause, then take the decision yourself.
tips: The delay was attributed to a change in the rules.
That final call was made by me.

items.situation: State the rule for every new model before release.
tips: Every new model must be reviewed before release.

It was escalated the same day it appeared.

items.situation: Give the credit for this quarter's result to your team, in one sentence.
tips: The credit should be shared with the whole team.
The framework was designed by four engineers.

items: Round 1 -- Guided
In three sentences, report one result from this quarter. Use the past passive once, the present perfect passive once, and one modal passive.
Round 2 -- The impact summary
Give a one-minute summary of one project: what was delivered, what has been completed, and what must still be reviewed.
Round 3 -- Name the agent
Deliver the same summary again, but add 'by + person' twice: once to give credit, once to take responsibility.
Curveball
A director asks 'So who made that call?' Answer in the active voice, then return to the passive for the impact.

answerkey.title: Reveal the model summary
list: Model: 'The approval process was streamlined last quarter, and two deliverables have been completed ahead of schedule. One issue was escalated to the vice president the same day it appeared, and the rationale is explained on page two. Every new model must be reviewed before release, so nothing is shipped without oversight. The credit should be shared with the whole team -- the framework was designed by four engineers. That final call was made by me.'
Past passive: The approval process was streamlined... / One issue was escalated...
Present perfect passive: Two deliverables have been completed...
Modal passive: Every new model must be reviewed... / The credit should be shared...
By + agent: ...was designed by four engineers. / That final call was made by me.
answerkey.note: Passive = be + past participle. The tense changes on 'be' only. Add 'by' when the doer is the point -- to give credit or to take responsibility. Switch back to the active voice the moment a person has to be named.

listenings.text: Here is the short version of the quarter, and I will keep it to sixty seconds. The approval process was streamlined last quarter, and two full weeks were cut from the cycle. Two deliverables have been completed ahead of schedule. One issue was flagged in March. It was escalated to the vice president the same day it appeared, and the rationale for that call is explained on page two of the memo. Going forward, the rule is simple. Every new model must be reviewed before release, and nothing is shipped without oversight. The daily checks are delegated to the team leads, so the work does not sit on one desk. And the credit should be shared with the whole team, because the framework was designed by four engineers, not by one manager.

Let me give you one test before you write a single sentence. Ask yourself what the reader should notice first: the result, or the person who produced it. If the answer is the result, use the passive. The approval process was streamlined. Two deliverables have been completed. The reader sees the impact immediately, and nobody has to be named. But there is a line, and you must not cross it. When something goes wrong, the passive becomes a place to hide. Mistakes were made. You have heard that sentence, and you know exactly what is wrong with it. Nobody is named, so it sounds like cover, not precision. So here is my rule. Use the passive for results, and switch back to the active voice the moment responsibility has to be attributed to a real person. If that person is you, say so. That decision was made by me.
